title: A church needing reform
hookLine: voices across the church agreed it needed reform; the sale of indulgences became the spark
tomorrow: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)

cards: A procession comes into a German town square: banners, candles, a cross, and in the middle, a papal document. A preacher calls out: give toward the building of a great church in Rome, and receive a letter of indulgence.
For yourself. Even for your mother and father, who have died. People push forward with coins.
And a little rhyme goes around, one that tradition puts in the mouth of a preacher named Tetzel: as soon as the coin in the box rings, a soul out of purgatory springs.

teach.h: A DEBT THAT STILL NEEDS HEALING.
teach.b: First, what an indulgence is in Catholic teaching, because the word is easy to mock and harder to explain.
When a sin is confessed and forgiven, Catholics say, its guilt is taken away, but some of its damage can remain, a kind of debt that still needs healing, in this life or in purgatory.
An indulgence is the church releasing some of that debt, drawing on the goodness of Christ and the saints, for someone who prays, makes a pilgrimage or does a good work.
Giving to the poor or to a church could be one of those works.
A gift became a price. Preachers sold letters from town to town, some promising far more than the church taught, and the money ran to building projects and to people's pockets.
The Bible already had a word for buying holy things.

In Acts, a man named Simon offers the apostles money for the power of the Spirit, and Peter answers, in the King James Bible: "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money."
People inside the church were already saying it needed reform: preachers, scholars like Erasmus, bishops, councils, ordinary believers.
Catholics would later forbid the selling of indulgences, while still teaching what indulgences are. Reformed Protestants later had a saying for today's line: the church must always be reformed.
And much later, the Second Vatican Council spoke of the church as always in need of being purified. The disagreement that comes next is real.

teach.h: THE HUNGER FOR REFORM WAS SHARED.
teach.b: But the hunger for reform was not only Protestant.

how: The Catholic Church still teaches about indulgences and grants them for prayer, pilgrimage and works of charity, never for sale; Protestant churches do not use indulgences, and some Reformed churches use the saying 'always reforming' about themselves.

o: the church's release from debt left after forgiven sin
a payment that buys forgiveness for any sin
permission from a priest to skip a church rule

p: release from a debt after forgiveness
the coin rings, a soul springs

s: in Catholic teaching, an indulgence forgives a sin in advance
it releases some of the debt that remains after a sin is already forgiven.

games.q: you're in the town square. the preacher says a coin will buy a letter of indulgence for your mother, who died last winter. what do you do?
o: go and ask your priest what it really means.
games.why: people paid, for themselves and for their dead. soon a monk who heard their confessions began asking hard questions about it.

practice: Name one thing in you that needs reform: a habit that has slowly turned from a gift into a price, something begun for good reasons that now runs on autopilot, on fear or on money.
Don't punish yourself for it; name it plainly, the way you'd name a crack in a wall you mean to fix. If you pray, hold it before God; if you don't, hold it in the light for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, the church's release from some of the debt that remains after a sin is forgiven. Its sale became the spark for the reformations.

carryVoice: Your line: always reforming. Reform can begin with one crack in one wall. See you tomorrow.
